newsitem.title: USA: Accused pilot's relatives hopeful over trial delay.
newsitem.headline: Accused pilot's relatives hopeful over trial delay.

text.p: Relatives of the first female B-52 bomber pilot said on Wednesday they were hopeful after her trial was halted while Air Force authorities review her request for an honourable discharge.
Lt. Kelly Flinn, who is 26 and single, requested the discharge in order to avoid being court-martialed on charges including adultery.
"It (the delay) was something that we had actually hoped for," Flinn's brother Donald Jr., said in an interview on NBC.
"At this point in time Kelly is very optimistic," Flinn's mother Mary said. "She would still love to fly for the Air Force, so she is trying to keep all her options open."
The Air Force said in a terse statement on Tuesday that it delayed the court-martial to allow Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall an opportunity to review Flinn's request.
Maj. Joe LaMarca, an Air Force spokesman in Minot, declined to comment on how long the court-martial would be delayed. But it was clear that Flinn's resignation bid was on the fast track.
It took only one day for the request to make its way through the chain of command to Widnall's office, instead of the standard three to four months. A decision from Widnall could come at any time.
"My guess is this particular resignation is probably going through the chain of command faster than any resignation in the history of the Air Force," Flinn's lawyer Frank Spinner said on Tuesday.

Flinn's lawyers stepped up their media campaign last week, arguing she was being unfairly persecuted for something commonplace in civilian life. But Air Force officials said the matter boiled down to broader violations of the code of conduct, including disobeying a direct order and lying during an official investigation.
Meanwhile, supporting players in the drama have started to air their sides in the public arena.
A man who identified himself as Flinn's ex-lover said on Tuesday Flinn knew that his marriage was still intact when she slept with him, calling into question her version of the story.

The comments were made by a caller on CNN's "Talk Back Live" television programme who identified himself as Marc Zigo, with whom Flinn has acknowledged having an affair. She is also accused of having an affair with an enlisted man.

"I do want to make perfectly clear she did know I was married. She had dinner with myself and my wife and friends while I was in Minot, North Dakota ... She was well aware of the marriage," Zigo said.

Flinn has said in recent interviews that Zigo lied to her about his marriage, telling her that he had legally separated from his wife, Airman Gayla Zigo. But in a letter sent to Widnall and obtained by reporters, Gayla Zigo painted Flinn as an uncaring homewrecker.

"Less than a week after we arrived to the base, Lt. Flinn was in bed with my husband having sex," Gayla Zigo wrote. "Lt. Flinn did not care about my feelings. She was just out for herself ... Lt. Flinn knew we were married and not separated, but that did not stop her."

All players in the case, as well as the dozens of journalists camped out in Minot, will now wait for the Air Force's decision. Widnall could offer Flinn an honourable discharge, a general discharge or a dishonourable discharge.
Flinn has said she will only accept an honourable discharge and that she will take her chances with a court-martial if she is offered anything less.
Unnamed Pentagon officials said on Monday that Flinn was unlikely to receive an honourable discharge, but that was before political leaders began weighing in on the issue.

Senate Republican leader Trent Lott said on Tuesday he believed Flinn was being "badly abused" by the Air Force and pledged to take the issue up with Defence Secretary William Cohen if the case moves ahead to a court-martial.
"I don't understand why she is being singled out and punished the way she is. I think at a minium she ought to get an honourable discharge," the Mississippi Republican said.
Conviction on adultery charges in a military trial is punishable by penalties that could range from a dishonourable discharge to fines and imprisonment.
Critics have argued Flinn's case highlights a double-standard in the way the U.S. Armed Forces treats the issue of adultery among its male and female staff.
